intro: Berlin protects around 600 individual trees as Naturdenkmäler, and most of them are oaks: pedunculate oaks planted by foresters, princes and protestors across four centuries in a city that has been besieged, bombed and divided more than once. Three of these stand in the Tegel Forest alone, home to the capital's record holders for oldest and thickest tree. The rest range from a Louisiana swamp cypress growing in a Prussian palace garden to an oak vandalized as a political protest against the Kaiser it was planted to honor. Most are free to see.
meta_description: Berlin's ancient trees range from an 800-year oak older than the city to a Louisiana swamp cypress in a Prussian palace garden. Mostly free to visit.
question_answer: Berlin's oldest tree is Dicke Marie, a pedunculate oak in the Tegel Forest whose age is genuinely disputed: the city's forestry office estimates 800 to 900 years, while a 2021 survey by the German Dendrological Society's heritage-tree board put it at a more conservative 500 to 600. It stands on the lakeside path near Tegel harbour, a 12 to 15 minute walk from the Alt-Tegel U-Bahn station.
question_meta: Berlin's oldest tree is a disputed 500 to 900 year old oak in the Tegel Forest. Where it stands, and the city's most remarkable trees.
question_context: Two credible sources disagree on Dicke Marie's age by several centuries, which is unusual even for a tree this old: Berlin's forestry office has long cited 800 to 900 years, while the German Dendrological Society's own National Heritage Tree board reassessed it in 2021 and concluded 500 to 600 was more defensible, since internal decay makes precise dating impossible either way. This page states both rather than picking the more dramatic number. What is not disputed is the tree's identity: two Humboldt brothers, Alexander and Wilhelm, are said to have named it after their family cook around 1800, while summering nearby at Schloss Tegel, and the nickname stuck for over two centuries. On 9 July 2021 Dicke Marie became the first forest tree in Germany named a National Heritage Tree. It stands in the Tegel Forest on the northeastern tip of Tegeler See, reached on foot from the Alt-Tegel U-Bahn station via the harbour bridge and lakeside path. A short walk further into Schlosspark Tegel stands the Humboldteiche, a younger but far thicker oak that is sometimes confused for the record holder; the two are neighbours, not the same tree.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Berlin?
faq.a: Dicke Marie, a pedunculate oak in the Tegel Forest. Its age is disputed: the city's forestry office estimates 800 to 900 years, while a 2021 heritage-tree survey concluded a more conservative 500 to 600.

faq.q: Are Berlin's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: Most are free to see without a ticket. Two locations need paying for access: the Treskow Plane, which grows inside Tierpark Berlin and requires a zoo ticket, and the four oaks on Pfaueninsel, reached only by a short paid chain ferry (6 euros as of April 2026) since the island itself is car-free. A fifth Pfaueninsel-area tree, a London plane by the ferry dock, stands on the free mainland side and needs no ticket at all.

A legally protected natural monument, a designation Berlin has used since 1939 (with a comprehensive ordinance update in 2021) for around 600 individually registered trees, plus a small number of glacial boulders, chosen for age, size, rarity or historical significance.

faq.q: Why are so many of Berlin's protected trees oaks?
faq.a: Pedunculate oak is the single most common species on Berlin's natural monument register, ahead of plane, chestnut and beech. Oaks tolerate the region's sandy Brandenburg soil better than most large trees and were the default choice for royal foresters, estate owners and municipal planners alike for centuries.

trees.name: Dicke Marie

location.address: An der Malche, Tegeler Forst, 13507 Berlin

trees.story: Berlin's oldest tree is older than the city itself. When Berlin got its first written mention in 1237, this pedunculate oak in the Tegel Forest had likely already been growing for over a century, its germination dated to around 1107. How much older it has grown since is a genuine dispute. Forestry officials have long put it at 800 to 900 years. In 2021 the German Dendrological Society's own National Heritage Tree board reassessed the same trunk and came back with a more conservative 500 to 600, arguing that internal decay makes anything more precise a guess. Both numbers can't be right, and this project would rather say so than pick the more impressive one. What isn't disputed: two teenage brothers who summered nearby at Schloss Tegel, Alexander and Wilhelm von Humboldt, are said to have named the tree after the family's cook around 1800, and the joke outlived them both. Goethe reportedly rested in its shade in 1778. The oak has grown gnarled and hollow rather than tall, topping out at just 15 to 16 metres, its bulk going into a trunk nearly six metres round instead. On 9 July 2021 it became the first forest tree in Germany named a National Heritage Tree, a small formal honor for something that was already, by any count, the oldest living thing in a city of 3.8 million people.

trees.name: The Humboldt Oak

location.address: Schlosspark Tegel, Adelheidallee, 13507 Berlin

trees.story: The thickest trunk in Berlin does not belong to the city's oldest tree. It belongs to its neighbour. A few hundred metres from Dicke Marie, inside the grounds of Schloss Tegel, this pedunculate oak has swollen to 7.80 metres around, wider than Dicke Marie despite being younger by centuries: 400 to 500 years old rather than 800 or more. It takes its name from the same family who has owned Schloss Tegel since 1766 and still does today, one of the few noble German estates that never left its original bloodline. Alexander von Humboldt, the naturalist whose name later ended up on a university, an ocean current and a squid, grew up walking past this oak on his way to the lake. Berlin listed it as a natural monument in 1939, protecting a crown that now spans 18 metres, wide enough to shade a tennis court. The palace itself only opens to visitors on Mondays between May and September, but the park around it, this tree included, stays open year round until sunset, for a suggested one euro donation left at the gate. Stand under it and you are looking at more wood, by circumference, than anywhere else in the German capital, a record that has nothing to do with age at all.

trees.name: The Steinlanke Oak

location.address: Große Steinlanke, Grunewald, 14193 Berlin

trees.story: Grunewald's oldest tree survived storms that took its own crown apart. Foresters put its age at 350 to 400 years depending on which survey is cited, a girth measurement that grew from 6.48 metres in 2018 to a commonly quoted 6.70 metres more recently, either of which means it was standing before Prussia existed as a kingdom. It grows at the Große Steinlanke, a quiet inlet of the Havel on the forest's western edge, its trunk gnarled and visibly weathered, the upper crown thinned by what local foresters describe as probable lightning strikes accumulated over centuries. A small sign near the Großes Fenster clearing, by the volunteer lifeguard station, points visitors to it, one of the few individually marked trees in a forest better known for its total size than any single specimen. Grunewald is Berlin's largest contiguous forest, threaded with lake paths popular with swimmers and joggers in summer, and this oak predates every villa and boathouse now standing near it. Reaching it takes real effort: the nearest train station, Wannsee, is nearly an hour's walk away, so most visitors take the 218 bus toward Theodor-Heuss-Platz and finish on foot along the shoreline. Nothing about it looks spectacular from a distance. Up close, the girth and the storm damage written into its upper branches tell a longer story than any plaque could.

trees.name: The Swamp Cypress of Charlottenburg

best_time.label: late October, when it drops its needles like a deciduous tree, the habit that confuses visitors expecting a conifer to stay green

location.address: Schlosspark Charlottenburg, Spandauer Damm, 14059 Berlin

trees.story: A swamp tree from the American South has spent two centuries in a Prussian palace garden. This bald cypress, native to the flooded river bottoms of the southeastern United States, went into the ground in Schlosspark Charlottenburg around 200 years ago, most likely during Peter Joseph Lenné's redesign of the grounds into an English-style landscape park. It has grown to five metres around and over 15 metres tall, dropping its needles every winter like a deciduous tree despite being a conifer, a habit that confuses first-time visitors expecting evergreen. Berlin protects it as a natural monument for a reason that has little to do with its size: its aging, partly hollow wood now shelters the hermit beetle, a rare, EU-protected species that depends on old, decaying timber exactly like this to survive at all. You are now more likely to help that beetle by leaving a tree standing than by planting a new one. The palace itself, the largest surviving Hohenzollern residence in Berlin, charges admission for its state rooms, but the gardens are free and open daily, the formal French parterre near the palace giving way further back to Lenné's looser, English-style paths, where this cypress stands among other 19th-century imports the royal gardeners tested against Berlin's winters. Most of them did not last two centuries. This one has.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the conifer that drops all its needles each winter, on a trunk five metres round. It stands in the looser English section of Schlosspark Charlottenburg, about a hundred metres from the carp pond elm.

trees.name: The Great Elm of Treptower Park

location.address: Treptower Park, near the Rosengarten, 12435 Berlin

trees.story: The newest tree on Germany's national heritage register has its roots in a river. This European white elm, standing directly on the Spree's bank in Treptower Park, was declared a National Heritage Tree only on 25 September 2025, one of the most recent additions to a small national list that otherwise mostly honors trees for age or scale alone. This one earns its place partly through rarity: Ulmus laevis is a floodplain elm scarce enough in Germany that a healthy 250-year-old specimen counts as remarkable regardless of size. Its roots reach directly into the Spree, drawing on a water supply few park trees get, which foresters credit for a vigor unusual in a tree this old. The trunk measures 6.35 metres around and the crown rises 25 metres, making it one of the largest trees in a park better known for its Soviet war memorial than its vegetation. It stands near the Rosengarten, a short walk from the boat landing, easily found by anyone walking the riverside path instead of heading straight for the monument. Dutch elm disease wiped out most of mainland Europe's mature elms across the twentieth century, a fungus spread by bark beetles that killed trees by the millions. This species, less favored by those beetles than the more common field and Wych elms, simply kept growing while its relatives disappeared.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Treptower Park S-Bahn station (S8/S9/S41/S42/S85/S46)

trees.name: The Mahlsdorf Village Lime

best_time.label: late June, when the lime blossom scents the street

location.address: Hönower Straße 13, 12623 Berlin

trees.story: In 2021 Berlin's district register dropped two of Mahlsdorf's protected trees, a Balkan horse chestnut and a black poplar, from its list of natural monuments. A crooked, ten metre lime standing in front of the neighbourhood's oldest building was not one of them. The Mahlsdorf Village Lime, a small-leaved lime outside the old parish church on Hönower Straße, has been protected since 1993 for outright rarity rather than size, a designation it has now outlasted two neighbours to keep. Its age is put at a minimum of 300 years, with local historians tracing the planting to the 17th century. Height was never the point: centuries of storm damage bent and hollowed the crown instead of raising it, leaving a squat, mossy shape barely taller than the church roofline while its trunk swelled to a girth of 4.45 metres, wider than many trees three times its height. By 1995 the district judged the limbs unsafe to leave unsupported and spent 8,000 Deutsche Mark bracing them with steel cables and fencing the base, work that still holds the tree together today. It stands on the old village high street, beside a church that itself survived the Thirty Years' War and the 1945 bombing, two witnesses to the same stretch of road that outlasted the empire, kingdom and two republics built around them.
trees.access: Free, stands on public ground in front of the church on Hönower Straße, viewable at all times (a low fence protects the base and root area)
trees.transport: 10-12 min walk from Berlin-Mahlsdorf S-Bahn station (S5)

trees.name: The Treskow Plane

location.address: Alfred-Kowalke-Straße 29, Tierpark Berlin, 10315 Berlin

trees.story: The oldest tree at Berlin's Tierpark predates the zoo around it by roughly two centuries. This London plane, its branches so intertwined that some have fused into single, oval cross-sectioned limbs, was already standing when the grounds were still the pleasure gardens of Friedrichsfelde Palace, a Hohenzollern summer residence later owned by the agricultural reformer Johann Carl Sigismund von Treskow, whose name it now carries. Lichtenberg's environmental office estimated its age at 250 years in a 2015 survey, putting its planting sometime in the mid-1700s, two centuries before the palace grounds reopened as a public zoo in 1955. It has grown a trunk 4.65 metres around and a crown 20 metres wide, tall enough at 25 metres to be visible over the enclosures near it. Reaching it requires a Tierpark Berlin ticket, since it now stands inside the zoo's grounds rather than in an open park, an unusual condition for a tree on this list but not a disqualifying one: anyone can buy a ticket at the gate. Look past the animals for a moment and you are standing under a plane tree that has outlasted a palace, survived the transition from royal garden to public zoo, and kept growing through both.
trees.access: Paid entry (Tierpark Berlin zoo ticket required)
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Tierpark U-Bahn station (U5)
trees.notes: Naturdenkmal since 2 March 1993 for regional historical significance, with additional protection for distinctive character added 20 May 2021. Common name standardized to 'London Plane' per project convention for Platanus x acerifolia/x hispanica. Coordinates from the German Wikipedia infobox.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches grown together into single fused limbs, on a trunk 4.65 metres round and 25 metres tall. It stands inside the Tierpark, the oldest tree on the old Friedrichsfelde palace grounds.

trees.name: The Kaisereiche

location.address: Rheinstraße / Moselstraße, 12161 Berlin

trees.story: Someone tried to kill this oak as a political protest, and Berlin planted a replacement within weeks. The original Kaisereiche went into the ground on 22 March 1879, planted by a local publisher to mark Kaiser Wilhelm I's 82nd birthday and golden wedding anniversary, at what was then a traffic circle on the edge of the new suburb of Friedenau. In November 1883, five years after two separate assassination attempts on the Kaiser had given Chancellor Bismarck his pretext for the Anti-Socialist Laws, someone damaged the tree badly enough that it needed full replacement, an act read at the time as a protest against those same laws. The oak standing at the corner of Rheinstraße and Moselstraße today is that replacement, which makes it roughly 143 years old rather than the 147 the original planting date would suggest, a small but honest distinction most retellings skip. Berlin protects it as a natural monument, and in 2004 a Hohenzollern descendant, Franz Friedrich Prinz von Preußen, unveiled a plaque marking 125 years since the first tree went in. The intersection has no official street name of its own, but Berlin's transit map still labels the bus stop and taxi rank here Kaisereiche, a small act of memory that has outlasted the publisher, the Kaiser, and the empire both men served.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Schlosspark Britz

location.address: Alt-Britz 73, Schlosspark Britz, 12359 Berlin

trees.story: Berlin's oldest and tallest ginkgo survived something most of its European relatives never had to: being fashionable. Ginkgo biloba reached European gardens in the 18th century as a botanical curiosity, a living link to trees that grew alongside dinosaurs, and wealthy estates across the continent planted them as status symbols rather than for shade or timber. This one went into Gutspark Britz sometime between 1880 and 1890, when royal garden inspector Wilhelm Nahlop redesigned the grounds of a former manor estate into the landscape park still standing today. It has grown a trunk over three metres around and stands close to 20 metres tall, the largest ginkgo recorded anywhere in the German capital. Ginkgos are dioecious, meaning individual trees are strictly male or female, and this one's autumn performance is the reward for the wait: every leaf turns a uniform gold within days of each other in late October, then drops almost at once, rather than the gradual, patchy fade most trees go through. The palace itself, Schloss Britz, charges a small admission fee for its restored period rooms, but the surrounding Gutspark is free and open daily, its grounds having won a national landscape prize in 1997, decades after the ginkgo inside it had already quietly become the biggest in Berlin.
trees.access: Free (Gutspark); Schloss Britz's period rooms charge separate admission
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Parchimer Allee U-Bahn (U7), or bus 181 to Alt-Britz

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Tiergarten

location.address: Englischer Garten, Großer Tiergarten, near Altonaer Straße, 10557 Berlin

trees.story: A tree that can live 3,000 years in California has had 135 of them in central Berlin. This giant sequoia, planted in 1891 in the Englischer Garten section of the Tiergarten, arrived in Europe only decades after the species itself did: the first seeds reached the continent in 1853, imported from California just two years after the tree was formally described at all, setting off a brief craze among wealthy estate owners for what nurseries of the time marketed as Wellingtonia. Berlin's planting, in the city's largest and most central park, is modest by the standards of a species that can exceed 90 metres in its native range, but it remains one of the tallest and bulkiest conifers growing anywhere in the capital. It stands a short walk from Schloss Bellevue, the German president's official residence, in a section of the Tiergarten deliberately landscaped in the looser, informal English style rather than the geometric French gardens found elsewhere in the park. Two world wars swept through the Tiergarten in the twentieth century, and postwar Berliners felled most of the park's remaining trees for firewood during the famine winters that followed 1945. This sequoia, planted decades earlier by gardeners with no idea what the century ahead held, made it through anyway.

trees.transport: 10 min walk from Bellevue S-Bahn station, inside the Tiergarten's Englischer Garten section

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bulk of it, the heaviest conifer in the Tiergarten and among the tallest trees in Berlin. It stands in the Englischer Garten section near Altonaer Straße, a short walk from Schloss Bellevue.

trees.name: The Great Oak of Pfaueninsel

location.address: Pfaueninsel, Schlosswiese, 14109 Berlin

trees.access: Free to walk once on the island. The island itself is car-free and reached only by a short chain ferry from the Nikolskoer Weg landing (adult single ticket 6 euros as of April 2026, family ticket 12 euros); the castle interior (separate, recently reopened after 2021-2025 restoration) is a different ticket and not needed to see this tree.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then roughly a 10-15 minute walk into the island to the Schlosswiese meadow area
trees.story:
Pfaueninsel's oaks were already old when the island became a royal garden. In 1793, Friedrich Wilhelm II ordered the landscaping of this Havel island, and his court gardener kept the oak stand standing rather than clear it, because the trees were already a century old by then. This one, on the meadow near the Schloss, may be one of those originals: at 565 to 567 centimetres around, it was until recently the largest and most striking oak on the island, its short trunk splitting low into one main stem and five curving limbs.

Nobody has measured its age directly, so a range is the honest answer here: somewhere between 200 and 400 years, bracketed from the island's own history rather than a bore sample. What is on record is a more recent event. Surveyors who examined the tree later criticized a crown reduction carried out on it, describing the pruning as unnecessary and unprofessional work on a specimen that deserved better handling.

The island itself has stayed almost untouched since. Pfaueninsel is reachable only by a short chain ferry, has no cars, and keeps the eighteenth century pleasure-garden layout Friedrich Wilhelm II laid out around trees like this one. Peacocks still roam it, the reason for the name. Walk the meadow near the Schloss and this is the oak the Prussian court gardener chose to save.

trees.name: The Tuereiche (Door Oak) of Pfaueninsel
trees.species: Sessile Oak (Quercus petraea) per monumentaltrees.com; Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) per baumkunde.de, an unresolved species conflict

location.address: Pfaueninsel, near the Schloss, 14109 Berlin

trees.access: Free to walk once on the island, reached only by the chain ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, the same crossing as the island's other oaks.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then a walk into the island near the Schloss.
trees.story:
Somebody built a working door into this oak's trunk, and it is still there. The Tuereiche, the Door Oak, stands near the Schloss on Pfaueninsel, its 5.58 metre girth measured just once, in 2017, by a tree registry that has not been back since.

Two sources agree on its size and disagree on its species. One calls it a pedunculate oak, the other a sessile oak, working from what looks like the same underlying survey rather than two independent looks at the tree. Berlin's own list of protected trees on the island names four sessile oaks and no pedunculate ones, which tips the balance without settling it outright.

Its age, about 250 years by the registry's estimate, is a guess made honestly: nobody has cored it, and the door itself, whatever its original purpose, carries no date of its own. What is certain is the island around it. Pfaueninsel became a royal retreat in 1793, and Friedrich Wilhelm II's gardeners built the new landscape around oaks that already stood there, this one very possibly among them.

Reach it by the same short ferry that serves the rest of the island's oaks, then walk toward the Schloss. Look for the door before you look for the tree. Most visitors do it the other way round and miss it entirely.

Species is genuinely disputed between the two sources (see species field); Berlin's official register lists only sessile oaks among Pfaueninsel's four designated NDs, which weakly favours that reading without settling it (this pass's register match below settles it outright: 6-101/B is filed as Quercus petraea, no disagreement on the register side). Last dated confirmation of life is from 2019. CONFIRMED 2026-08-07 against data/registers/berlin-naturdenkmale.json: this is ND 6-101/B ('Pfaueninsel, ca. 100m nordoestlich vom Faehranleger', register coords 52.430667/13.122139, about 12m from this entry's own coordinates).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the working door built into its trunk, 5.58 metres round. It stands near the Schloss on Pfaueninsel, among the island's other oaks.

trees.name: The Pond Oak of Pfaueninsel
trees.species: Sessile Oak (Quercus petraea), per Berlin's official Naturdenkmal register
trees.age_estimate: undocumented; likely 100-300 years, inferred from the island's wider oak stand

location.address: Pfaueninsel, north of the Wasservogelteich (waterfowl pond), 14109 Berlin

trees.access: Free to walk once on the island, reached only by the chain ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, the same crossing as the island's other oaks.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then a longer walk to the northern part of the island near the Wasservogelteich.
trees.story:
The most precise thing known about this oak comes from a stranger's holiday photo. In May 2024 a visitor uploaded a picture of a wide-crowned oak north of the Wasservogelteich, Pfaueninsel's waterfowl pond, and the phone's own GPS placed the tree more accurately than any register description on file.

Berlin's protected-tree list already knew it existed: one of four sessile oaks on the island carrying legal Naturdenkmal status, described only by compass bearing and a rough distance from a landmark. No age is recorded anywhere, and none should be invented, though the island's oak stand generally predates the royal garden built around it from 1793.

What the photo confirms is that the tree is alive, healthy and exactly where the register said it should be: a wide, well-formed crown branching low over the path. It sits far enough from Pfaueninsel's other two documented oaks, roughly a kilometre, that it will not fit into the same five-minute stop, but the whole island is under a kilometre long, an easy single walk that takes in all three.

Same ferry, same island, further into it: past the Schloss and toward the pond, where deciduous woodland shelters some of Pfaueninsel's least visited but longest-standing residents.
trees.notes: Pinned via a geotagged Wikimedia Commons photo (File:Pfaueninsel_Oak.jpg, CC BY 4.0, S. Makhin, taken 2024-05-19), whose EXIF coordinates agree with Berlin's official Naturdenkmal register description (ND 6-103/B, 'north of the Wasservogelteich') to within about 10m. No age recorded by either source.

photo.attribution: S.Makhin, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide crown branching low over the path. It stands north of the Wasservogelteich, the waterfowl pond, about a kilometre deeper into Pfaueninsel than the island's other two registered oaks.

trees.name: The Ferry Landing Plane

location.address: Pfaueninselchaussee 100, west of the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel, 14109 Berlin

trees.story: Three of Pfaueninsel's protected oaks require a ferry ticket. This plane tree does not. Berlin's Naturdenkmal register lists it at Pfaueninselchaussee 100, the address of the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel, the old inn that has stood at the mainland ferry dock since long before the chain ferry became the island's only public access. The oaks across the water needed the eighteenth century royal garden that grew up around them to survive this long; this plane needed nothing more than the road leading to the crossing point, protected for its beauty and its tie to the place rather than for age or rarity, the reason the district gives on its own designation record. No planting date survives, and no second source beyond the government ordinance has turned up despite real searching, an honest gap rather than an invented history. What makes it worth including anyway is the position: anyone heading for the Pfaueninsel oaks passes directly beside it, on the free side of the water, before they have paid for anything at all. See this one on the way in, whether or not the ferry crossing that follows fits the day.
trees.access: Free, and no ferry ticket required: this tree stands on the mainland side of the crossing, by the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel restaurant and ferry dock, unlike the island's other protected oaks, which need a paid ferry.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then under 5 minutes on foot to the ferry landing area
trees.notes: Berlin Naturdenkmal register_id 6-71/B, designated 1993-03-02, reason given as 'Schoenheit, landeskundliche Gruende' (beauty, regional-historical significance), not age or rarity, so no age is claimed. Only one source found: the register (and the underlying berlin.de ordinance PDF, which is the same government designation read twice, not a second independent source). Two verify passes searched baumkunde.de and monumentaltrees.com (403-blocked) for a tree-specific second source; none found. Commons geosearch within 250m returned nothing, so no dated photo confirms current vitality; treat as likely standing but unconfirmed. Location finding worth keeping: the register address (Pfaueninselchaussee 100) is confirmed via ADAC Maps and pfaueninsel.de as the mainland ferry-dock side, not the island, so this tree is free to see without a ferry ticket.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one plane among Pfaueninsel's registered trees, and the only one on the mainland side of the water. It stands beside the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel at Pfaueninselchaussee 100, by the ferry dock.

trees.name: The Cut-Leaf Oak of Pfaueninsel
trees.species: Sessile Oak, cut-leaf variety (Quercus petraea var. laciniata)

location.address: Pfaueninsel, roughly 150m northeast of the Schloss, 14109 Berlin

trees.story: Forty five metres from Pfaueninsel's Great Oak stands a second, stranger oak that Berlin protects for an entirely different reason. Where its famous neighbour earned Naturdenkmal status for size and disputed age, this one is registered for rarity alone: a cut-leaf sessile oak, Quercus petraea var. laciniata, a naturally occurring variety with deeply dissected, almost fern-like foliage instead of the plain oval leaf every other oak on the island carries. The two trees stand close enough that a visitor could assume the register was describing the same tree twice. It is not. The government ordinance that protects both lists them under separate numbers, at separate coordinates, for separate reasons, one for its bulk, the other purely because its leaf shape almost never occurs in the wild. No age is recorded for this one at all, since rarity rather than antiquity is the whole case for protecting it, and no source beyond the designation record itself has been found describing this specific tree. Find the Great Oak first, then look forty five metres further for its odd, deeply cut cousin, the rarer of the two despite standing in its more famous neighbour's shadow.
trees.access: Free to walk once on the island, reached only by the chain ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, the same crossing as the island's other oaks.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then roughly 10-15 minutes into the island to the area northeast of the Schloss, close to the Great Oak.
trees.notes: Berlin Naturdenkmal register_id 6-108/B, designated 1993-03-02, reason 'Seltenheit' (rarity) for the cut-leaf variety specifically ('Geschlitzblaettrige Trauben-Eiche' in the ordinance text). Distinctness confirmed against the already-published ber_011 (45m away, register 6-102/B): baumkunde.de's entry for ber_011's exact coordinates describes an ordinary crown with no cut-leaf note, while the ordinance separately and specifically designates 6-108/B for its dissected foliage at a distinct coordinate, so these are two real trees, not one register duplicate. Only one source found (the register/ordinance, one government designation read two ways, not two independent sources); two verify passes searched baumkunde.de, ostdeutsches-baumarchiv.de and monumentaltrees.com (403-blocked) without finding a tree-specific second source. Commons geosearch within 100m returned nothing, so no dated photo confirms current vitality; treat as likely standing but unconfirmed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves, unlike the plain oval leaf of every other oak on the island. It stands forty five metres from the Great Oak, roughly 150 metres northeast of the Schloss.

trees.name: The Lietzensee Plane

location.address: Lietzenseepark, north shore near Wundtstrasse 56, 14057 Berlin

trees.story:
This plane added 43 centimetres to its waistline in ten years. Measured at chest height it went from 6.00 metres in 2015 to 6.43 metres in 2025, which by circumference makes it the sixth thickest tree on record anywhere in Berlin. A laser measurement in 2025 put its height at 22 metres.

The date usually given for its planting is 1807, an estimate rather than a ring count. That would make it a sapling in an occupied city, the year after Napoleon's army marched through the Brandenburg Gate and took the Quadriga off the top of it to Paris. Everything around the tree arrived later. Lietzenseepark is a twentieth century arrangement of terraces and lakeside paths, laid out around trees that were already big when the surveyors turned up.

Berlin protects it as a natural monument under the number 4-26/B, which is the city saying in administrative language that nobody touches this one. It was photographed alive and in full leaf in May 2025.

The register keeps no age and no girth of its own, so both figures above come from the volunteer surveyors who have been measuring it every five years, which is also how anyone knows it is still growing. From here the shore path runs about 170 metres to a Caucasian wingnut, the other reason this lake is on the map.
trees.access: Free, public park (Lietzenseepark)
trees.transport: Sophie-Charlotte-Platz or Kaiserdamm (U2), about 10-12 minutes' walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single trunk, 6.43 metres round and 22 metres tall, the sixth thickest tree recorded in Berlin. It stands on the north shore of the Lietzensee, about 170 metres along the path from the wingnut.

trees.name: The Lietzensee Wingnut

location.address: Lietzenseepark, northeast section near Lietzenseeufer 5, 14057 Berlin

trees.story:
Berlin has five Caucasian wingnuts on record, and this one is not yet a hundred years old. The planting date on file is 1927, which by the standards of most trees on this map is recent, and it is not why anyone stops here.

The shape is. The trunk breaks into several stems close to the ground, so the surveyors who measured it gave up on the usual chest height and put the tape around the base instead: 5.94 metres at ground level, a figure they flagged themselves as flattering, because a fork counts as girth in a way a single trunk never does. What it produces is a tree that reads as a small grove growing out of one root plate.

Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the Caucasus and northern Iran, where it grows in wet ground along rivers, which is why it has done so well on the edge of a Berlin lake and why it is a rare thing in the drier planting beds of the rest of the city. In midsummer it hangs chains of winged nutlets, half a metre long, off the tips of every branch.

Berlin protects it as natural monument 4-25/B. The most recent published photograph of it dates from June 2015 and the register listing has carried it since, so if you find it changed, tell us. The Lietzensee plane stands about 170 metres along the same shore.

best_time.label: July and August, when half-metre chains of winged nutlets hang from every branch tip

trees.access: Free, public park (Lietzenseepark)
trees.transport: Sophie-Charlotte-Platz or Kaiserdamm (U2), about 10-12 minutes' walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk splitting into several stems close to the ground, so it reads as a small grove on one root plate. It stands in the northeast corner of Lietzenseepark, 170 metres from the single-trunked plane.

trees.name: The Karpfenteich Elm

location.address: Schlosspark Charlottenburg, southeastern corner of the Karpfenteich, Spandauer Damm, 14059 Berlin

trees.story:
Nobody knows how old this elm is, and that is the honest answer rather than a gap waiting to be filled. Berlin protects it as natural monument 4-27/B at the southeastern corner of the carp pond behind Charlottenburg Palace, and neither the city register nor the surveyors who have measured it twice will put a year on it.

What is on record is size and a near standstill. Its trunk was 4.85 metres around in 2015 and 4.88 metres in 2020, roughly six millimetres of growth a year, the pace of a tree that finished the growing part of its life a long time ago. A laser put it at 21.5 metres tall in July 2020.

The species is the reason to look twice. European white elm is uncommon in city plantings, and Dutch elm disease has taken most of the big elms across the continent over the past century, so a mature one of this girth is a survivor rather than a specimen.

Its address helps. The grounds were laid out in the 1690s as the formal garden of Sophie Charlotte's summer palace and later loosened into an English landscape park, and the carp pond it stands on belongs to that second version. The swamp cypress at the other end of the same park is about a hundred metres away. The last published photographs of the elm were taken in February 2015 and July 2020.
trees.access: Free, public park (Schlosspark Charlottenburg)
trees.transport: Richard-Wagner-Platz (U7) or Sophie-Charlotte-Platz (U2), about 12-15 minutes' walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.88 metres round and 21.5 metres tall, on an elm where most of Europe's big elms are gone. It stands at the southeastern corner of the carp pond behind Charlottenburg Palace.

photos.note: The fluted bole with its buttress roots, the 4.88 m trunk the story is about. It was this tree's lead photograph until 2026-09-13, when a whole-tree frame from the same shoot took that place under the Cadiz standard, crown and trunk both readable rather than bark filling the frame. Kept beside the lead rather than thrown away.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Fraenkel Garden

location.address: Landhausgarten Dr. Max Fraenkel, Luedickeweg 1, 14089 Berlin-Kladow

trees.story: Berlin declared this copper beech a natural monument in 1993, growing inside Landhausgarten Dr. Max Fraenkel, a garden the banker Fraenkel commissioned around 1930 on the Havel shore at Kladow, on ground that had been a brickworks. He hired Erwin Barth, then the city's director of gardens, who laid out a formal rose garden, a perennial-lined cascade and fruit and vegetable plots close to the house, then a looser landscape section further out with a waterfall, ponds and a tea pavilion. The garden changed hands and use across the rest of the century before Spandau's district authorities restored it and reopened it to the public in 2016, with a visitor centre standing where a private family once entertained guests. The beech carries the register's protection for beauty and local historical interest, but no source yet gives its age or girth, so both stay open questions for whoever measures it next. It stands somewhere within the garden's 2.97 hectares, free to walk and easy to reach from central Berlin, on the same route the BVG ferry and the weekend cyclists take out to Kladow. Its crown, dark purple against the garden's greens, is one more layer in grounds that were built up in stages across nearly a century.
trees.access: Free, the garden is open to the public with a visitor centre (restored and reopened 2016)
trees.transport: BVG ferry F10 to Alt-Kladow, or bus, then a walk to the garden on Luedickeweg
trees.notes: Register point (52.442538,13.128787) sits roughly 270m from the garden's own mapped grounds (OSM way, centroid 52.4443295,13.1314394); pinned to the garden itself rather than the raw register coordinate, and marked approximate accordingly. Register is the only source for the tree's own designation criteria; berlin.de (district) and berlingarten.de corroborate the garden's history and public status but are not tree-specific. No age or girth found for this individual beech. Do not confuse with the different 120-year-old Blutbuche Naturdenkmal at the Kladow-Center (a separate tree, separate designation, covered in 2019 berliner-woche.de coverage about crown pruning); that is a different location entirely.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dark red leaves against the garden's greens. It stands somewhere within the 2.97 hectares of the Landhausgarten Dr. Max Fraenkel, which the register does not narrow down further.

trees.name: The Podbielski Oak

location.address: Olympischer Platz 3, behind the Preussenturm at the Osttor (East Gate), Olympiastadion Berlin, 14053 Berlin

trees.story: The only tree standing anywhere on the Olympiastadion's 810 by 320 metre grounds carries the name of a Prussian cavalry general. In 1914 organisers at the old Deutsches Stadion marked Victor von Podbielski's seventieth birthday by naming an oak there after him. What happened to that oak is disputed. Berlin's own account of the stadium describes today's tree as roughly 200 years old, its name simply carried forward when the Nazi-era Olympiastadion replaced the earlier ground for the 1936 Games. A local history site tells a harder story: that the original Podbielski oak was felled along with the old stadium, and a replacement planted in 1936 to carry the name into the new arena. Both readings agree on what stands there now: a protected oak behind the Preussenturm at the Osttor, alone on a site built for 100,000 spectators and otherwise stripped of trees. It has stood through the 1936 Olympics, the Second World War and everything the stadium has hosted since, a scrap of green on concrete built for propaganda. It is free to see from outside the stadium fence, or reachable at the trunk with a stadium ticket.
trees.access: Free to view from outside the stadium fence at the Osttor (East Gate); stadium entry (paid, roughly EUR 7) lets visitors stand beside it
trees.transport: U2 Olympia-Stadion, about 500m / 6 minute walk to the Osttor (East Gate)
trees.notes: Register (4-6/B, designated 1993-03-02) gives species as Quercus petraea and the same coordinates as de.wikipedia's district Naturdenkmal list, which is not independent of the register (same ordinance) but corroborates the pin. Age genuinely disputed between two independent sources: de.wikipedia's Olympiastadion article implies continuity from a c.1820s original ('etwa 200 Jahre alt'), golocal.de says the 1914-named original was felled with the 1913 Deutsches Stadion and a replacement planted in 1936 (~90 years old); both recorded rather than picking a winner. A Commons photo filename ('Westend Olympiastation Stieleiche.jpg') suggests possible confusion with Quercus robur (Stieleiche); not resolved this pass, register's Quercus petraea kept as the recorded species. monumentaltrees.com 403'd throughout, no girth recorded.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the only tree on the whole Olympiastadion site, 810 metres by 320 and otherwise bare. It stands behind the Preussenturm at the Osttor, visible from outside the fence.

trees.name: Berlin's Tallest Tree
trees.age_estimate: documented planting in 1843, roughly 180 years old

location.address: Mühlenweg, southern Tegeler Forst, near the junction with Heiligenseer Weg, 13505 Berlin-Tegel

trees.access: Free, in the public Tegeler Forst (Landschaftsschutzgebiet). No gate or ticket; reached on forest trails.
trees.transport: No direct public transport; nearest station is Alt-Tegel (U6), then roughly 3km (35-40 min walk or a short cycle) into the forest along the Heiligenseer Weg trail. The Revierförsterei Tegelsee has placed a visible marker sign on the trail pointing to the tree.
trees.story:
For decades Berlin's tallest tree was the wrong tree. The record belonged to the Burgsdorff Larch, planted in 1795 by the forester whose name it carries and measured by climbers at 45 metres in 2000 and 42.5 in 2012. Then an airborne laser survey scanned the city's forests in 2021 and put the larch at 41.05 metres. The same scan found a beech 180 metres to the west standing at 43.15, and the title changed hands. Regional press reported the new holder in October 2022 and RBB television filmed it a year after that. The larch itself came down in a storm in June 2025.

Nothing on the ground announces any of this. The beech has no register entry and no protection order, and no name has stuck to it: Friedensbuche and Hohe Buche have both been floated and neither took. Forestry records date its planting to 1843, which makes it about 183 years old, no age at all beside the yews and oaks elsewhere on this site, and quite enough to have stood through the German Empire, two world wars and the forty years when this forest sat at the edge of West Berlin. Its trunk measures 96 centimetres across, so roughly three metres round, which is unremarkable. Height is the whole argument here.

The Tegelsee forestry office has put a sign on the trail pointing at it, which helps more than it sounds: a stand of tall beeches gives away nothing about which one is tallest.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the forestry office's marker sign on the trail, which points straight at it, and by a trunk of only 96 centimetres across. It stands in the Tegeler Forst where the Muhlenweg meets the Heiligenseer Weg.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.name: The Englischer Garten Wingnut

location.address: Grosser Tiergarten, Englischer Garten, near the Teehaus, Berlin

verified_sources: berlin-naturdenkmale.json register_id 1-39/B (Land Berlin Naturdenkmal register, DL-DE-Zero 2.0)
trees.access: Free, public park (Grosser Tiergarten)
trees.transport: Bellevue (S-Bahn), roughly 5-8 minutes' walk
trees.story:
Berlin protected this tree in 1993 on two stated grounds, Eigenart und Schönheit, character and beauty, and recorded nothing else at all. No age, no girth, no planting date. Natural monument 1-39/B gives a species and a point in the Englischer Garten, and there the paperwork stops.

The species carries the rest. Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the Caucasus and northern Iran, where it grows in wet ground along rivers, which makes it an awkward fit for the drier planting beds of Berlin and explains why almost nothing else in the city looks like it. In midsummer it hangs chains of winged nutlets off the branch tips, half a metre long. Berlin's better known wingnut stands across the city on the shore of the Lietzensee, planted in 1927; by the account of the one Berlin writer who went looking for this one, in 2022, this is the bigger of the two, already tall and broad and still filling out.

It stands in good company. Ten more protected trees sit within about three hundred metres of it, the Tiergarten's giant sequoia among them, which is a dense run of natural monuments for the middle of a capital city.

Nobody has dated it, so nobody can honestly say what it has stood through. If you know when it went in, or you have had a tape around it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the chains of winged nutlets it hangs in summer, half a metre of them at a branch tip. It is the tall, broad-crowned tree in the Englischer Garten a few steps from the white Teehaus.

best_time.label: July and August, when half-metre chains of winged nutlets hang from the branch tips

trees.name: The Queen's Oak of the Englischer Garten

location.address: Grosser Tiergarten, Englischer Garten, near the Teehaus and its pond, Berlin

trees.access: Free, public park (Grosser Tiergarten)
trees.transport: Bellevue (S-Bahn), roughly 5-8 minutes' walk
trees.story:
Queen Elizabeth II planted this oak herself, on 27 May 1965, on her first visit to West Berlin. The sapling was reportedly raised from stock at Windsor Castle. Almost nothing else on this map arrives with its planter, its provenance and its exact date all written down.

What she put in the ground was an American tree. Quercus rubra, the Northern Red Oak, is neither British nor German, and it has taken to the Tiergarten well: roughly twenty metres now, with a crown that has come up lopsided rather than round. It went into a divided city and has spent most of its life in a reunited one, which is more history than sixty-one years usually buys. By oak standards it is barely started.

Finding it is the part that takes effort. Neither newspaper account gives a coordinate, and there is no register entry to fall back on, because this one was never listed as a natural monument. Both accounts put it near the white Teehaus, and the more recent is precise about the last few metres: to the right of the path, on the way down to the pond. That is as close as anyone has written it down, which is why the pin here points at the teahouse rather than at the trunk.

Nobody has taped its girth either. If you stand in front of it, tell us where you were standing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, each lobe ending in a bristle where the Tiergarten's own oaks are rounded, and by a crown grown up lopsided on a twenty-metre tree. It stands right of the path from the white Teehaus down to the pond.

trees.name: The Oak of the Kleistpark

location.address: Heinrich-von-Kleist-Park, east of the Verfassungsgerichtshof (Kammergericht), on the oval lawn, 10781 Berlin

trees.access: Free, public park (Heinrich-von-Kleist-Park), open daily
trees.transport: U-Bahn Kleistpark (U7), 2 min walk
trees.story:
Berlin's official reason for protecting this oak is beauty. The Naturdenkmal order of 2 March 1993 lists it as 7-15/B, a Stiel-Eiche on the oval lawn east of the Kammergericht, and gives two grounds: Schoenheit, and regional-historical interest. No girth, no height, no age. The city looked at it and decided that was enough.

The ground under it has the longer record. Heinrich-von-Kleist-Park was Berlin's first botanical garden, from 1801 until 1903, when the collection was lifted and moved out to Dahlem. A monument on the same lawn still marks what used to stand here. The colonnades and the court building came later, and the lawn stayed open, which is why the oak is visible whole instead of crowded into a hedge.

It is not the largest tree in the park. That is the wingnut, and a bald cypress and a ginkgo grow nearby; two further protected trees stand here as well, a catalpa at the Potsdamer Strasse entrance and a mulberry. But a children's tree walk written with the district's own green-spaces office stops at this one and puts it plainly: here we have a thick, large oak, and it is a Naturdenkmal.

Nobody has dated it. The Berlin register carries no age field for any of its trees, and no other source has filled the gap. If you know when this one went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick oak trunk on the oval lawn east of the Kammergericht building, the same lawn that holds the monument to the park's former botanical garden. The park's bigger wingnut stands elsewhere.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Twin Yews of Johannaplatz

location.address: Johannaplatz (northern part of the hexagonal garden square), 14193 Berlin

trees.access: Free, public garden square (Gartendenkmal), open at all times
trees.transport: About 15 min walk from S-Bahn Grunewald (S7)
trees.story:
Berlin protected both of these yews for one stated reason: beauty. They hold separate entries in the register, 4-30/B at the south end of the square and 4-31/B at the north, both Taxus baccata, both signed off on the same day in March 1993, and the ground given for each is Schoenheit. Nothing about size, nothing about age.

The square under them was laid out in 1890 for a church that never got built. Six streets of the Grunewald villa colony run into it, and the hexagon left in the middle went to the gardeners rather than the architects. In 1896 the royal garden inspector Hermann Roehr redesigned it as a garden square, with groups of broadleaves and conifers set around semicircular seating, and in 1898 it was named after Johanna von Bismarck, the chancellor's wife. The borough writes that the old tree stock here has been largely preserved to this day.

The two yews stand at opposite ends of that hexagon, roughly sixty metres apart, which makes them one stop rather than two. Yews give little away. Dark, dense and slow, they are the species most often underestimated by people who judge a tree by its waistline.

Neither of these has ever been dated, and the Berlin register records no girth for either. If you have put a tape round one of them, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the dark evergreen pair standing at opposite ends of the hexagonal garden square, about sixty metres apart. The pin marks the northern yew; its twin holds the south end, where six Grunewald streets meet.

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination
trees.transport: Podbielskiallee or Dahlem-Dorf (U3), roughly 10 min walk
trees.story:
This is the third Caucasian wingnut on this list, which says more about nineteenth-century German gardeners than it does about the Caucasus. Berlin protected it on 2 March 1993 as natural monument 6-40/B and recorded almost nothing else: a species, a place, no age, no girth.

The place is the point. From 1903 until 1966 these grounds in Dahlem were the Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the Prussian state's teaching institute for gardeners, where the planting was the syllabus. Species came here to be studied, which is how a walnut relative from the forests between the Black Sea and the Caspian ended up behind what is now a computing institute. The school closed, the garden went quiet for decades, and TU Berlin restored it between 2012 and 2014 as a teaching garden again.

Late summer is when a wingnut declares itself. The seed chains hang out of the crown in strings up to forty centimetres long, each nut carrying two papery wings, and nothing else in this garden does anything remotely like it. The leaves are long and pinnate, closer to an ash than to the walnut it is actually related to.

Nobody has dated this one and nobody has published a girth for it. If you have put a tape round the trunk, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long strings of winged seeds hanging out of the crown in late summer and the ash-like pinnate leaves. It stands at the south-western corner of the grounds, behind the Zuse Institute building.

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.name: The Yew of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination

trees.story:
Of all the protected trees in this garden, the yew is the one with the longest future. Taxus baccata is the slowest and longest-lived tree in northern Europe, unremarkable at five hundred years, an age at which an oak already counts as ancient and a birch has been gone for centuries.

This one stands in the front garden of the old Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the Prussian gardeners' school that held this Dahlem block from 1903 to 1966 and taught planting by planting. Berlin listed the yew as natural monument 6-76/B-1 on 2 March 1993 and the western red cedar a few paces away as 6-76/B-2, on the same day, under the same ordinance. The paperwork treats them as a pair and so does the ground.

Yews hand a visitor almost nothing. Dark, dense, fluted at the base rather than round, with bark that peels in red-brown strips, and effectively impossible to date from outside, because the heartwood rots away while the tree carries on growing perfectly well. That is why Britain's yew estimates swing by a thousand years and why nobody has offered a number for this one.

Berlin records no age and no girth here. If you have measured it, we would like the figure.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the dark evergreen needles and the red-brown bark peeling in strips, the only yew on these grounds. It stands in the front garden off Koenigin-Luise-Strasse, a few paces from the tall western red cedar.

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.name: The Giant Thuja of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination

trees.story:
Germans call this species the giant tree of life, Riesen-Lebensbaum, and Berlin used exactly that name when it put this one under protection as natural monument 6-76/B-2 on 2 March 1993. The register offers the name and no measurement, so treat the word giant as the species talking rather than a surveyor.

The species earns it at home. Thuja plicata grows in the wet coastal forests of the Pacific Northwest, where it passes sixty metres and a thousand years, and where the coastal nations of British Columbia built canoes, longhouses, boxes and woven clothing out of a single tree. Almost nothing else on that coast rots as slowly. European nurseries wanted it from the 1850s onward, and a Prussian school for gardeners was precisely the sort of address that would take one.

This tree stands in the front garden of the former Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the teaching institute that ran here from 1903 to 1966, beside the yew protected on the same day. Close up it is unmistakable: flat fanning sprays of scale leaves, fibrous bark running in vertical ribbons, and a pineapple smell when you crush a sprig.

Nobody has recorded its age or its girth. Both are the kind of thing a visitor with a tape measure could settle in a minute.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flat fanning sprays of scale leaves and the fibrous bark running in vertical ribbons, the only western red cedar here. It stands at the north end of the grounds, next to the protected yew.

trees.name: The Juniper of the TU Schaugärten
trees.species: Juniper (Juniperus virginiana or Juniperus scopulorum; sources disagree on which)

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination
trees.transport: Podbielskiallee or Dahlem-Dorf (U3), roughly 10 min walk
trees.story:
Two official-looking sources quote the same protection number for this tree, 6-77/B-1, and name two different junipers. Berlin's own natural monument register calls it a Virginischer Wacholder, Juniperus virginiana, the eastern redcedar that grows from Nova Scotia down to Georgia. The German Wikipedia list of protected trees in Steglitz-Zehlendorf calls the same entry a Zypressen-Wacholder, Juniperus scopulorum, the Rocky Mountain juniper of Colorado and Alberta. Roughly two thousand kilometres of North America separate them in the wild.

That disagreement is not carelessness so much as the nature of the two trees. Both are American junipers with blue-green scale foliage, shreddy bark and small waxy berry-cones instead of woody ones, they hybridise freely where their ranges meet, and telling them apart in a garden is a job for someone holding a hand lens rather than a clipboard.

It stands at the southern edge of the old Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the Prussian gardeners' school that occupied these grounds from 1903 to 1966, near the Altensteinstrasse side. A teaching collection is exactly where an unresolved American juniper would end up, and exactly where the label matters.

Berlin protected it on 2 March 1993 and has never published an age or a girth for it. If you can settle which juniper this is, from the foliage or the cones, we would rather have your answer than pick one.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the blue-green scale foliage and the small waxy berry-cones, the only juniper among these protected trees. It stands at the south-eastern corner of the grounds, towards Altensteinstrasse.

trees.name: The Saucer Magnolia of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination

trees.story:
The saucer magnolia was invented by a retired cavalry officer of Napoleon's army who had decided that growing things was a better use of a life than burning them. Etienne Soulange-Bodin crossed two Chinese magnolias at Fromont near Paris around 1820 and got a tree that flowered young, tolerated cold clay and opened its goblets before the leaves came out. Europe has been planting it ever since. Every saucer magnolia in Berlin descends from that idea.

This one sits on Berlin's protected list as natural monument 6-77/B-2, the Tulpen-Magnolie, signed off on 2 March 1993. It stands on the western side of the old Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the Prussian gardeners' school that ran here from 1903 to 1966 and whose grounds TU Berlin brought back as a teaching garden between 2012 and 2014.

For ten days in April it is the loudest thing in the garden, and the protected conifers a hundred metres away are not in the conversation: pink and white flowers the size of a fist, hundreds of them, on bare grey branches. Then the leaves arrive and it goes back to being a broad, quiet, low-branching tree for another year.

No planting date has ever been recorded for this individual, and nobody has published a girth.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in April by the pink and white goblet flowers opening on bare branches, the only magnolia among the protected trees here. It stands on the western side of the grounds, behind the Zuse Institute.

best_time.label: April, when the flowers open on bare branches before any leaf

trees.name: The Swiss Stone Pine of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination
trees.transport: Podbielskiallee or Dahlem-Dorf (U3), roughly 10 min walk
trees.story:
A Swiss stone pine belongs at two thousand metres, on the Alpine treeline, in the last thin band of soil before the rock wins. This one is growing on Berlin sand at fifty metres above sea level, and it has been doing it since 1903.

That date is not a guess from the garden's founding. TU Berlin, whose vegetation technology department runs these grounds, says of the Pinetum framing the old rose garden that its Oriental spruce, its Zirbelkiefer and its Weymouth pine still date from 1903, naming the species one by one. Counting forward puts this pine at roughly 120 years, which for a species that regularly passes five hundred in the Alps is early middle age.

The Zirbelkiefer arrived here as teaching material. From 1903 until 1966 the site was the Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the Prussian state's school for gardeners, and a conifer collection was a working textbook. In the Alps this tree feeds an entire economy of its own: the nutcracker bird buries its seeds and forgets enough of them to plant the next forest, and what the bird misses goes into schnapps.

A storm in February 2022 took two trees over a hundred years old off these grounds, and the account of it names neither. This Zirbelkiefer was still standing in November 2024, a hundred and twenty-one growing seasons after it was put in.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the dense, stiff, dark crown, quite unlike the open blue-green Weymouth pine at the other end of the garden. It stands at the north-eastern end, in the conifer group around the old rose garden.

trees.name: The Katsura of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination
trees.transport: Podbielskiallee or Dahlem-Dorf (U3), roughly 10 min walk
trees.story:
For two weeks in October the ground under this tree smells of gingerbread. Drying katsura leaves give off maltol, the same compound that comes out of a hot oven, which is why German named the species Kuchenbaum and Lebkuchenbaum, cake tree and gingerbread tree. You smell it before you work out where it is coming from.

It is probably the largest katsura in Berlin. That is not our measurement but the judgement of Professor Norbert Kuehn, who heads the TU Berlin department that maintains this garden and who opens his own account of the place by naming this tree first. Berlin had already protected it on 2 March 1993 as natural monument 6-78/B, the Japanischer Kuchenbaum.

The species came out of Japan and China into European gardens in the later nineteenth century, arriving in time for a Prussian teaching institute to want one. From 1903 to 1966 these grounds were the Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt, the state school for gardeners, and every rarity here was bought to be studied rather than admired. Katsuras usually rise as several stems from low down instead of one trunk, and the round heart-shaped leaves come out bronze-pink in April, go blue-green by June and finish apricot.

No age has ever been published for it, and the register records no girth.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small round heart-shaped leaves, several stems rising from low down, and the smell of gingerbread under it in October. It stands at the eastern edge of the grounds, near the conifer group.

best_time.label: October, when the leaves turn apricot and the ground underneath smells of gingerbread

trees.name: The Weymouth Pine of the TU Schaugärten

location.address: TU-Schaugärten (former Königliche Gärtnerlehranstalt), Königin-Luise-Straße 22, 14195 Berlin-Dahlem

trees.access: Free, TU Berlin's own Schaugärten (educational display garden, restored 2012-2014); TU Berlin's own site gives seasonal opening hours (April/May and Sept/Oct roughly 10am-8pm, June-Aug roughly 10am-10pm); no confirmed winter access found, so treat as a growing-season destination

trees.story:
This species was once a strategic asset. Eastern white pine grew straight and tall enough to mast a warship, so the British crown reserved the best New England specimens for the Royal Navy and branded them with a broad arrow, which colonists resented enough to riot about in 1772. Europe got its own trees instead, and named them after Lord Weymouth, who planted them at Longleat in the early 1700s. Germany still calls the species Weymouth-Kiefer.

This one dates from 1903. TU Berlin, whose staff maintain these grounds, records that the Pinetum around the old rose garden still holds its original Oriental spruce, Zirbelkiefer and Weymouth pine from that year, naming the three species directly, which puts this tree at roughly 120 years. That is the same year the Koenigliche Gaertnerlehranstalt opened here, the Prussian school where gardeners were trained until 1966.

Berlin protected it on 2 March 1993 as natural monument 6-84/B. It stood through the Battle of Berlin, the closing of the school in 1966 and the long stretch afterwards when these grounds were no longer anyone's classroom, until TU Berlin restored them between 2012 and 2014. A storm in February 2022 brought down two trees over a hundred years old here; the account does not say which two. This pine was photographed standing in November 2024.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the soft blue-green needles in bundles of five, the long curved cones and the open crown in horizontal layers. It stands in the southern half of the grounds, towards Altensteinstrasse.

trees.story:
This oak is protected by law for one reason only: Berlin has hardly any others like it. The city's register lists rarity and nothing else, which is fair. Quercus libani comes from the mountains of the Near East, from Lebanon and Syria into Turkey, and a grown specimen in the middle of the Tiergarten is a long way from home. Berlin made it Naturdenkmal 1-36/B on 2 March 1993.

It does not look much like the oaks around it. Its leaves are long and narrow, edged with small bristle-tipped teeth, closer to a sweet chestnut's than to the rounded lobes of a native oak. This corner of the park lets you check that for yourself. A pedunculate oak protected on the same day grows a short walk east, and Queen Elizabeth II's red oak of 1965 stands about 80 metres off. Three oaks from three continents, within a few minutes of each other.

Nobody has published its age or its girth, and here that leaves a real question open. In the hungry winters after 1945, Berliners cut most of the Tiergarten down for firewood, and the park was replanted from 1949. Whether this tree came through that or arrived with the replanting, no source we have found says. If you know, or you have a tape measure with you, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, long and narrow with small bristle-tipped teeth like a sweet chestnut's rather than an oak's rounded lobes. It stands east of the English Garden, about 80 metres from the Queen's red oak.

trees.story:
Every leaf on this tree is two colours: dark green on top, silver-white felt underneath, so the crown flickers pale whenever the wind turns it over. That underside is where the silver lime gets its name, and it is why Berlin protects this one for its beauty. The register gives regional heritage as the second reason, and made it Naturdenkmal 1-90/B on 2 March 1993.

It is not a Berlin tree by birth. The species is native to south-eastern Europe and Anatolia, so a grown one in the Tiergarten was planted by somebody on purpose, and nobody has recorded who or when.

Its neighbour is another arrival. The Bismarck Monument, Reinhold Begas's bronze chancellor, stood in front of the Reichstag until 1938, when it was moved here to the Grosser Stern to clear the ground for Hitler's plans for the capital. The statue came with a date. The tree did not.

The moment to come is July. Silver limes flower weeks after the city's common limes have finished, and the scent carries well past the trunk, which tends to bring the bees before it brings the people.

There is no age and no girth for this tree in any source we have read. If you know when it was planted, or can put a tape round it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, dark green above and silver-white underneath, which show pale when the wind turns them. It stands near the Bismarck Monument on the north side of the Grosser Stern.

trees.story:
German calls this tree the Flatter-Ulme, the flutter elm, after flowers that hang on stalks long enough to shake in a breeze. In English it is the European white elm, and it is one of the few elms that is genuinely at home here: the species belongs to the river floodplains of central and eastern Europe, the kind of wet lowland Berlin is built on.

That matters more for an elm than for most trees. Dutch elm disease took most of Europe's elms in the twentieth century, and the white elm came through better than its relatives, because the bark beetles that carry the fungus tend to pass it over. A grown one in a city park is still worth stopping for.

Berlin protects this one for its Eigenart, its distinctiveness, and made it Naturdenkmal 1-38/B on 2 March 1993. The register does not say what struck the people who chose it, so you will have to decide that for yourself on the spot. It has company: a pedunculate oak protected the same day stands about 55 metres away, a silver lime about 85, and a Lebanon oak just beyond them, a small grove of separately listed trees east of the English Garden.

Nobody has published its age or its girth. If you have a tape measure with you, we would like the number.

trees.story:
Of the protected oaks in this corner of the Tiergarten, this is the only one whose species belongs here. Within a couple of hundred metres stand a Lebanon oak from the Near East and a red oak from North America that Queen Elizabeth II planted in 1965. This one is Quercus robur, the pedunculate oak, the oak of the Brandenburg lowlands and of the Tiergarten itself, which began in the sixteenth century as the Electors' hunting forest.

That does not make this tree a survivor of the forest, and nothing we have read says it is. The Tiergarten has been landscaped, relandscaped, and after 1945 largely cut down for fuel and replanted from 1949. Where this oak sits in that story, no source records.

What the city did record is that it is worth keeping. Berlin made it Naturdenkmal 1-37/B on 2 March 1993, for its distinctiveness and its beauty, two reasons where many protected trees get one. A white elm listed the same day stands about 55 metres away.

It is easy to tell from its famous neighbour. The Queen's oak has leaves ending in sharp bristles and acorns that sit tight to the twig; this one has rounded lobes, and acorns that hang on long stalks, which is what pedunculate means.

No age or girth has been published. If you can measure the trunk, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the rounded leaf lobes and acorns on long stalks, unlike the bristle-tipped leaves of the Queen's red oak 125 metres away. It stands east of the English Garden, about 55 metres from the protected white elm.

trees.story:
Berlin protects this katsura for three reasons at once: beauty, rarity and regional heritage. It became Naturdenkmal 1-43/B on 2 March 1993, and it stands on Altonaer Strasse, diagonally across from the Hansabibliothek.

The setting is half the reason to come. The Hansaviertel was rebuilt for the Interbau exhibition of 1957 as a showcase of modern architecture, and the address the register gives, Altonaer Strasse 6, is a long apartment block raised off the ground on V-shaped concrete stilts. The katsura grows up in front of its balconies, a single tall trunk with a bright green crown reaching several storeys up the facade. Whether it was planted with the building, nobody has recorded, so we will not guess.

The species comes from Japan and China, and it saves its best for October. The small heart-shaped leaves turn apricot and gold, and as they dry on the ground they give off a smell of burnt sugar, strong enough that German calls this the Kuchenbaum, the cake tree. Two more katsuras are on our map in Berlin, one in the TU Schaugärten and one in the Tiergarten south of the Fauler See.

The tree stands on the green in front of a residential block, and we have not confirmed whether that ground is public, so look at it from the street. No age or girth has been published. If you know either, tell us.

trees.story:
In October the air under this tree smells of burnt sugar. Katsura leaves give off the scent as they colour and dry, which is why German calls the species the Kuchenbaum, the cake tree. You tend to smell it before you have worked out which tree it is coming from.

The katsura comes from Japan and China, and in Berlin it is a rarity by the register's own word. The city made this one Naturdenkmal 1-35/B on 2 March 1993, for its beauty and its rarity, and the register places it precisely: north of the Strasse des 17. Juni, south of the Fauler See. That pond, at the western end of the Tiergarten, is a protected nature area, and the tree stands between it and the traffic on the great east-west axis.

The rest of the year it is a quieter tree, with small rounded heart-shaped leaves that open with a reddish tinge in spring and stay a soft green through summer. October is when it earns the walk, as the crown goes apricot and gold.

trees.story:
This oak was planted to mark a battle, one year to the day after it was fought. On 2 September 1871, the first anniversary of the Prussian victory at Sedan, a young pedunculate oak went into the ground at Zehlendorf's village crossroads and called it a Friedenseiche, a peace oak, for the end of the Franco-Prussian War. A bronze plaque on the south side of the trunk still says so.

That makes it one of the few trees on this map with a birthday. It is about 155 years old, and it has had a busy junction for company the whole time. Beside it stand the old village church and the Heimatmuseum Zehlendorf; around it the village became a suburb, the suburb became part of Greater Berlin, and after 1945 it ended up in the American sector of a divided city. Berlin made the oak Naturdenkmal 6-31/B in 1993.

Traffic has been the hard part. In June 2020 a heavy limb broke off and came down in the middle of the rush hour. The response was to give the roots more room: the sealed ground around the trunk was to be opened up, and the bench that used to circle it was taken away.

So do not expect to sit under it any more. Stand at the corner of Potsdamer Strasse and Berliner Strasse instead, and read the plaque.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bronze plaque on the south side of the trunk. It stands on its own at the junction of Clayallee, Potsdamer Strasse and Berliner Strasse, beside the old village church and the Heimatmuseum.
