trees.story:
Berlin protects this one because almost nobody else has one. The city's register names rarity first, and Fontanesia earns it: a quiet relative of the privet and the olive, native to Asia Minor and almost never planted in a German park. Most people crossing Moabit's Kleiner Tiergarten walk past it as just another shrub.

That is the reason to look. It is not here for size, and the register makes no claim that it is. It was made a Naturdenkmal on 2 March 1993 for two reasons, rarity and what Berlin calls landeskundliche Gründe, local-history grounds, a phrase the city uses for trees that tell you something about the place they stand in. The register does not spell out what that something is here, and we will not guess.

There are two of them. Berlin lists them separately, as 1-49 and 1-50, about 25 metres apart on the east side of Stromstrasse, and a visitor sees them as a pair, so we treat them as one stop. Both were photographed in leaf in June 2024, which is the best evidence we have that they are still doing well.

What nobody has recorded is how old they are or how big. Berlin's register carries neither age nor girth, and no other source we found fills the gap. If you know when these were planted, or you have stood beside them with a tape measure, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its narrow, privet-like leaves on a shrub-sized tree. It stands east of Stromstrasse with its twin, listed as 1-50, about 25 metres further east.

trees.story:
Most of Berlin's protected trees made the list for being rare, old or tied to the city's history. This one was protected for its looks. When Berlin named it Naturdenkmal 1-42/B on 2 March 1993, the register gave a single reason: Schönheit, beauty.

It is a tulip tree, a North American species, and it stands on the Luiseninsel, a small island inside the Grosser Tiergarten reached along the park's own paths. That is a fitting address for a tree judged on appearance, because the tulip tree is one of the easiest in the world to tell apart once you know the trick. Its leaves look as if someone took scissors to them: four lobes and a flat, notched tip where every other leaf would come to a point. In early summer it carries upright cups of pale green and orange that give the species its name, often high enough that you notice the fallen petals before the flowers.

It was photographed in full leaf in May 2024, so it is alive and well, and it is the only tulip tree among the Berlin trees we map.

What the register does not give is an age or a girth; Berlin's Naturdenkmal records carry neither, and we found no other source that dates it. If you know when it was planted, or you have measured the trunk, tell us.

trees.story:
Botanists knew this tree as a fossil before anyone knew it was still alive. The dawn redwood was described from fossil remains in 1941, and only a few years later living trees turned up in central China. Seed went out to gardens around the world from 1948, which is how a species once thought extinct ended up in a park in Wedding.

That history sets a ceiling on its age, if not a number. A dawn redwood in a Berlin park cannot predate that postwar seed, so this one is decades old rather than centuries, and its claim to a page is rarity and looks rather than years. Berlin agreed: it made the tree Naturdenkmal 1-44/B on 2 March 1993 for both, Schönheit and Seltenheit, beauty and rarity.

It stands in the Volkspark Rehberge, opposite the entrance to the open-air stage, and it is a conifer that behaves like an oak. Its soft needles come out bright green in spring and turn a rusty orange-brown in autumn before they drop, leaving a bare, tapering frame all winter. It was photographed in leaf in June 2025.

Berlin's register gives no planting date and no girth, and we have not found another source that does. If you know when it went in, or you have measured the trunk, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in autumn by its needles turning rust-orange, and in winter by its bare branches, a conifer without needles. It stands opposite the entrance to the Freilichtbühne, the open-air stage.

trees.story:
Berlin did not protect this maple for one reason. It gave four. When it became Naturdenkmal 1-102/B-2 on 2 March 1993, the register cited its character, its beauty, its rarity and local-history grounds, all at once.

The register calls it Bosnischer Ahorn, the Bosnian maple, and it is a form of the Italian maple from the mountains of southern Europe and the Balkans, not a tree you expect on one of the most visited squares in Berlin. It stands on the Gendarmenmarkt at the Charlottenstrasse corner, south-west of the Deutscher Dom.

It does not stand alone, and that matters if you come to find it. About 14 metres away is a Norway maple, registered beside it as 1-102/B-1, and from a distance the two read as a pair of ordinary maples. Up close they part ways. The Norway maple has broad leaves whose lobes end in fine sharp points. The Italian maple's leaves are smaller, with shallow, blunt, rounded lobes, which is what its subspecies name, obtusatum, means. Look at a leaf before you look at the trunk.

About 50 metres north is a third protected tree on the same square, a Japanese pagoda tree.

Nobody has published an age or a girth for this maple; Berlin's register records neither. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, smaller with blunt, rounded lobes, where the Norway maple 14 metres east has sharp-pointed ones. It stands at the Charlottenstrasse corner, the westerly of the two.

trees.story:
In German this tree is called the Geweihbaum, the antler tree, and in winter you can see why. The Kentucky coffeetree grows few, thick, blunt twigs, and once its leaves are down the crown looks less like a tree than a rack of antlers held up against the sky. It keeps that look for a long part of the year, because it is among the last trees to leaf out in spring and among the first to drop in autumn.

The English name comes from its seeds. Settlers in North America are said to have roasted them as a coffee substitute; the raw seeds and pods are toxic, so this is a story to enjoy rather than test.

Berlin made this one Naturdenkmal 1-53/B on 2 March 1993 for a single reason, rarity, and it is the only coffeetree among the Berlin trees we map. It stands on the Märkischer Platz, opposite Wallstrasse 53, and was photographed in leaf in May 2024. The leaves, when they come, are worth a look: each one is a doubly divided frond of many small leaflets, and a single leaf can reach the better part of a metre.

It also makes an easy pair with the velvet-leaf euodia on Fischerinsel, about 600 metres away.

Berlin's register records no age and no girth for it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its thick, sparse twigs, like antlers in winter, and in summer by huge leaves split into many small leaflets. It stands on the Märkischer Platz, opposite Wallstrasse 53.

trees.story:
Its German name is not flattering: Samthaarige Stinkesche, the velvet-haired stinking ash. Gardeners elsewhere call the same species the bee-bee tree, which is kinder and closer to the point. It flowers in high summer, after most trees have finished, with broad flat heads of small white flowers, and in July and August it can hum with bees from some distance away.

It is not an ash at all. Tetradium daniellii belongs to the citrus family and comes from northern China and Korea, and the stinking part of the name refers to the sharp smell of its crushed leaves. Berlin made this one Naturdenkmal 1-54/B on 2 March 1993 for beauty and rarity, and it is the only one among the Berlin trees we map.

It stands on Fischerinsel, the southern end of the Spree island in the middle of Berlin, level with the Australian Embassy at Fischerinsel 5. The tree is seen from the public street and green strip; the embassy grounds are not open, and you do not need them. It was photographed in leaf in May 2024.

It sits about 600 metres from the Kentucky coffeetree on the Märkischer Platz, so the two make an easy short walk between two rarities.

Berlin's register gives no age and no girth. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its ash-like leaves split into leaflets, and in July and August by flat heads of white flowers busy with bees. It stands on Fischerinsel, level with the Australian Embassy at number 5.

trees.story:
The Humboldt University keeps two protected ginkgos, one in each of its courtyards, and Berlin registers them as two separate natural monuments. This is the southern one, Naturdenkmal 1-6/B-1. Its twin, 1-6/B-2, stands about 60 metres to the north, in the other courtyard of the same building.

Berlin listed both on 2 March 1993. The reasons depend on who you ask. The state register gives beauty and regional heritage. The Wikipedia list of natural monuments in Mitte gives rarity and distinctiveness. That makes four reasons across two sources, and not one of them is age.

The moment to come is November. A ginkgo's whole crown turns butter gold and then drops its leaves in a day or two, so the window is short and easy to miss.

The tree also starts a short walk. A protected red horse chestnut stands in the forecourt a few steps away, and a protected London plane grows on Bebelplatz across the street, so three of Berlin's natural monuments sit within a couple of hundred metres of each other.

University courtyards are normally open by day, but we have not confirmed the hours, so check at the gate. Nobody has published an age or a girth for this ginkgo. If you have a tape measure and a minute, tell us what it comes to.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its small fan-shaped ginkgo leaves. It stands in the south courtyard of the main building at Unter den Linden 6; its protected twin is in the north courtyard.

Berlin's register files this tree as a Fleischrote Rosskastanie, a flesh-red horse chestnut, which is the German name for it and does the flowers no favours. In English it is simply the red horse chestnut: the same upright candles as the familiar white kind, in red, and less common.

Come in May. That is when a horse chestnut puts its candles up over the whole crown, and on this one they come out red rather than white.

It is also a stop on a very short walk. One of the university's two protected ginkgos stands in the south courtyard a few steps behind it, and a protected London plane grows on Bebelplatz across the road.

This is a conifer that goes bare every winter. A bald cypress grows needles like a pine and then, each autumn, turns them copper red and drops the lot. It is a rare tree in Berlin's parks, and this one, north of the rose garden in the Bürgerpark Pankow, is under state protection.

It is not the only one on our Berlin map. Another bald cypress stands in the palace garden at Charlottenburg, on the far side of the city, so a reader who likes this one has a second to find.

The Bürgerpark is free, about ten minutes on foot from S and U Pankow. Nobody has published an age, girth or height for this tree. If you have measured it, or know when it was planted, tell us.

This one was listed for its beauty and for natural-history reasons instead: for what it says about the species and the landscape rather than about the people around it.

The pin is a good one. The register gives a point for the tree itself, and the Wikipedia list of Pankow's natural monuments gives its own coordinate about 40 metres away, which for two sources in a park is close agreement. Walk the south shore path and look for it near the middle.

A poplar by water is in its element, and the Kreuzpfuhl is a pond ringed by a public park, free to walk around. It has no single day of glory. It is the kind of tree you come to because you know a native black poplar is a rare thing to find in Berlin.

The square in front of Berlin's natural history museum holds five protected trees, and the two that give the group its name are copper beeches, one off each wing of the building. The museum charges for what is inside. The square, and everything growing on it, is free.

Berlin's register lists them one by one. Naturdenkmal 1-75/B-1, designated on 2 March 1993, is the copper beech by the east wing, and it is where our pin stands. Its partner, 1-75/B-2, is by the west wing, about 70 metres across. A beech, 1-76/B, stands by the east wing too, another protected tree, 1-77/B, by the west, and an oak, 1-78/B, out on the square itself. The register gives the east-wing copper beech its place for beauty and for regional heritage.

We have mapped them as one stop rather than five, because that is how you will meet them: a single forecourt, all within about a hundred metres, a minute from the U-Bahn.

Copper beeches are worth seeing through the year. Their leaves open purple in spring, darken through the summer and turn copper before they fall, so the pair looks different with every visit.

No source gives an age, girth or height for any of the five. If you have measured one, tell us which, and what it came to.

trees.story:
Berlin's natural monument register lists more than six hundred trees, and only two of them are protected for four reasons at once. This oak is one. When the city made it Naturdenkmal 1-86/B on 2 March 1993, it cited distinctiveness, beauty, regional heritage and scientific grounds. Most entries in the register cite a single reason; only three in the whole list mention science at all.

It is a sessile oak, the less common of the two oaks in Berlin's parks. The pedunculate oak is the one you meet everywhere. This one stands at the corner of Scheidemannstrasse and the Grosse Querallee, near the Carillon in the Tiergarten.

The register's point marks the tree itself, and a photograph on Wikimedia Commons from May 2024 is titled with this exact place, Scheidemannstrasse at the corner of the Grosse Querallee, near the Carillon, so the pin is a firm one.

What the register does not say is what the scientific interest is. It records the reason and leaves the explanation out.

The Tiergarten is a free public park, open at all hours, about ten minutes on foot from the Hauptbahnhof, and the Tulip Tree of Luiseninsel is under a kilometre away if you want to keep walking.

No source we have found gives an age, a girth or a height. If you know any of those, or why scientists cared about this oak, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a sessile oak, its acorns sitting directly on the twig rather than on stalks. It stands at the corner of Scheidemannstrasse and the Grosse Querallee, near the Carillon in the Tiergarten.

trees.story:
Berlin's most famous traffic island holds a 67-metre column, a gilded Victoria and a protected tree from North America. The column itself is a transplant: it was moved here from in front of the Reichstag in 1938 and 1939, when the Nazi planners rebuilt the Grosser Stern as a showpiece junction. Whether this black locust was already growing on the island then, or went in afterwards, no source records.

The species has its own long road to Berlin. Robinia comes from the eastern United States and reached Europe in the early seventeenth century, through the Paris garden of Jean Robin, the French king's gardener, whose name the genus still carries. It took to the dry, sandy soils of Brandenburg so well that it now grows wild across them. Its wood is famously hard and its twigs carry paired thorns, and in early summer it hangs out clusters of white flowers that smell of honey and draw bees from a long way off.

The island sits in the middle of a busy five-way roundabout. You reach it on foot through the pedestrian tunnels under the traffic, which come up on the island itself.

Berlin lists the tree as Naturdenkmal 1-34/B and records nothing about its size or age. If you stand under it with a tape measure, send us the girth.

trees.story:
On the night of 15 January 1919, Freikorps soldiers shot Karl Liebknecht in the dark beside the Neuer See and reported that he had been killed trying to escape. A memorial stone by the lake marks it now. This London plane stands a short walk east of the water, south of the Grosser Weg, and nobody has recorded whether it was there to see any of that.

What it is, at least, is easy to say. The London plane is a city tree by temperament: it sheds its bark in flat plates, which is one reason it shrugs off soot and exhaust, and the shedding leaves a trunk patched in olive, cream and grey like old camouflage. In winter it keeps its seed balls, bristly brown spheres on long threads that hang on after the leaves have gone. Berlin planted the species along its streets by the thousand. Here, among the lawns and paths east of the lake, it has room to spread.

The Neuer See is one of the busiest corners of the Tiergarten, with a beer garden and rowing boats on the water, so this is a tree a lot of people walk past without knowing the city lists it. It is Naturdenkmal 1-56/B.

The register gives no age, girth or height. If you put a tape around the trunk at chest height, tell us what it says.

trees.story:
The London plane may not be from London at all. It is a hybrid of the oriental plane and the American sycamore, and the cross seems to have happened by accident in the seventeenth century, somewhere the two parents grew side by side. One theory puts it in a London garden; another in Spain, which is why botanists also call it Platanus hispanica. This one stands a few steps north of the Spanish Embassy, which is either a coincidence or the tree being diplomatic.

Its spot is a crossing: Lichtensteinallee meets the Grosser Weg here, two of the paths that thread the south-western Tiergarten towards the zoo and the Landwehr Canal. Hybrid vigour is part of why the London plane is everywhere in European cities. It grows fast, takes heavy pruning and poor soil, and puts up with air that kills more delicate trees. A plane in a park, with no kerb pressing on its roots, gets to show what it does when nobody is in its way.

Berlin protects it as Naturdenkmal 1-87/B. A second protected plane stands about 200 metres to the north-west, east of the Neuer See, so the two make an easy pair on one walk.

The register stops at the species and the spot. No age, no girth, no height. If you know any of them, or measure the trunk yourself, we would like to hear.

trees.story:
This oak grows on a strip of park squeezed between two kinds of water: the Neuer See on one side, the Landwehr Canal on the other. One is a park lake, with rowing boats in summer. The other was dug between 1845 and 1850 to carry barges around the crowded Spree, and still carries tour boats past the zoo today.

It is a pedunculate oak, the common oak of the north German lowlands, and probably the single most useful tree a park can hold. Oaks support more insect life than almost any other European tree, and the insects feed the birds: woodpeckers, nuthatches and jays all work an old oak. In a good year the ground beneath it fills with acorns on long stalks, the peduncles the species is named for, and jays carry them off, bury them and forget a good share.

Berlin protects it as Naturdenkmal 1-88/B, and a volunteer photographing the city's natural monuments for Wikimedia Commons left ten pictures of it, all taken within a few metres of the trunk.

What nobody has written down is how old it is or how big. If you walk the strip between the lake and the canal, a girth measurement would tell us a great deal.

trees.story:
Two protected oaks stand on this stretch of canal bank, about 25 metres apart, and Berlin lists them as separate natural monuments, 1-20/B and 1-97/B. Standing there, you will read them as one place: a pair of pedunculate oaks on the green strip along the Landwehr Canal, a few minutes from the zoo.

The street is named after Katharina Heinroth, and she is worth knowing about. A zoologist, she took over the Berlin Zoo in 1945, when the war had left it in ruins and fewer than a hundred of its thousands of animals were still alive. She rebuilt it over the following decade and was the first woman to run a German zoo. The bank that carries her name is a quiet one: a canal path, joggers, the odd tour boat sliding past.

Pedunculate oaks are the native oak of this lowland, the tree that carries its acorns on long stalks and its leaves on almost none. Whether these two were planted together, or one came long after the other, no source says.

The register records nothing about their age or size. If you measure either trunk, or better both, tell us which one and what you found.

trees.story:
Berlin's register and the photographer who has followed this oak through every season cannot agree on what it is. The register, which protects it as Naturdenkmal 1-95/B, calls it a pedunculate oak. That photographer, posting winter and summer pictures to Wikimedia Commons since 2024 and citing the city's own tree-cadastre number 17-229, calls it a sessile oak. Both are native here and they hybridise freely, so this is not a careless mistake on either side. It is a genuinely awkward question.

You can try to settle it yourself. A pedunculate oak hangs its acorns on long stalks and holds its leaves almost stalkless, with two small ear-like lobes where the leaf meets the twig. A sessile oak does the reverse: acorns sitting tight to the twig, leaves on a clear stalk and tapering at the base. Come in autumn and look at both.

The tree stands between the Bellevueallee and the Strasse des 17. Juni, the broad avenue named for the East German uprising of 17 June 1953, when workers across the GDR struck and Soviet tanks put them down. Schloss Bellevue, the German president's residence, is a few minutes away.

The register gives no age, girth or height. Tell us which oak you think it is, and if you can, how far round the trunk.

trees.story:
Berlin's register takes the trouble to say exactly which beech this is: Gewoehnliche Buche, Rot-Buche, the plain green common beech. The name trips people up. Rotbuche means red beech, but it refers to the pinkish timber, not the leaves, and the purple-leaved copper beech planted in so many old parks is a separate form. This one is the original, the tree that would cover most of central Europe if people let it.

That is not an exaggeration. Left alone, beech outcompetes nearly everything on ordinary soils, mostly by shade: its leaves are layered so tightly that very little light reaches the ground, and seedlings of other trees give up underneath it. The bark stays smooth and silver-grey into old age, which is why beech trunks across Europe carry carved initials that have stretched with the tree for decades.

Its spot is south of the Kleiner Stern, one of the path junctions in the eastern Tiergarten, and east of the Rosengarten. In late October and early November the crown goes from green to copper and orange, and the leaves that drop make a dry, rustling carpet that lasts most of the winter.

Berlin lists it as Naturdenkmal 1-96/B and records neither its age nor its size. If you can get a tape around the trunk, we would like the figure.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the crown turns copper and orange

trees.story:
This elm flowers in March, weeks before its own leaves, in small purple-brown tassels that dangle on threads and are easy to mistake for nothing at all. A white elm in flower looks faintly smoky against a pale sky, and most people crossing the bridge nearby will walk past without looking up.

Ulmus laevis is at home in river meadows and on wet ground, and the Tiergarten, laid out on the low, damp land along the Spree, gives it what it likes. Old trees of the species can do something few European trees do: grow plank-like buttresses at the base of the trunk, the kind of thing you expect in a rainforest rather than a Berlin park. Whether this one has started, the register does not say. You will have to look.

It is the second protected white elm in the Tiergarten on our map; the other stands east of the English Garden. A third registered elm, listed together with beeches, grows north-west of here near Tiergartenstrasse 30. Berlin knows this one as Naturdenkmal 1-92/B.

No age, girth or height has been recorded. If you measure the trunk, or find buttresses at its foot, send us what you see.

trees.story:
Berlin Zoo calls it the eternal oak, and says it has been giving shade for 500 years. If the zoo's figure is right, the tree was already old when the zoo itself opened in 1844, the first in Germany. The zoo also gives it a second name, the Columbus oak, without explaining it.

Treat the number as the owner's word rather than a measurement. It is a round figure, no method is given, and nobody has published a girth to check it against. A photograph of the tree on Wikimedia Commons is captioned the same way, about 500 years old. So the honest version is: about 500 years, according to the zoo.

There is a second thing we cannot quite close. Berlin's register protects one pedunculate oak inside the zoo, Naturdenkmal 1-52/B, south of the hippo house, listed in 1993 for its distinctiveness and for regional heritage. That is the tree we have mapped. It is the only protected oak the register lists in the grounds, which makes it almost certainly the eternal oak, but no source we have read says in so many words that the two are the same tree. The zoo counts eleven protected natural monuments on its ground in all.

You will need a ticket, and our pin comes from the register rather than from a visit, so expect to look around south of the hippo house. If you have stood under it, tell us whether we have the right one.
